samples.summary: Offline-copy recovery is offered even when the revocation reconcile failed, so content from a workspace the user was removed from can be re-materialized as a new server-side document
samples.evidence: `OfflineRuntime` runs the revocation reconcile in its own try/catch (offline-runtime.tsx:114-142) that logs and continues, then unconditionally runs `offerRecoverableWork` at line 146. `purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments` is the ONLY mechanism that reaches the removed member's own device — workspaces.ts:159 gates `removeMember`'s purge on `isOfflineUser(String(userId))`, which is false on the owner's machine, and the design records this explicitly (`workspaces.ts:147-155`: "The removed member's own device is reached by nothing that happens here... Until that session happens the content is on their disk"). The reconcile is skipped whenever `fetchDocuments()` throws — which is precisely the offline state this whole feature exists for, and is the deliberately-tested path (`offline-runtime.test.tsx:190-197`, "keeps sweeping when the reconcile fails", asserts `toastWarning` fires after `fetchDocuments.mockRejectedValue`). Attack/abuse chain: user A is removed from workspace W while holding an archive of a W document (archives are produced on `epoch-reanchor` / `document-purged` / `actor-mismatch`); A opens the app with the network unavailable or the listing 5xx-ing; the reconcile's `archives: "drop"` never runs; the recovery toast still fires and its "Save a copy" action calls `recoverOfflineCopy` -> `createDocument` + `applyImportedContent`, uploading the revoked workspace's document content back to the server as a document A owns. The design states the rule this violates in workspaces.ts:130-133 ("a deleted workspace ends the authority to read any of its content, and recovery would hand back a whole document from it") — the enforcement point just isn't on the recovery path's critical path. Fix shape: gate `offerRecoverableWork` on the reconcile having actually completed this session, or drop archives for ids not in the last successful listing before offering.

samples.summary: `load()` has no owner check while `loadArchive()` does — the store key is the only thing keeping one account's document bytes from another on a shared device, and every component of that key is derivable
samples.evidence: `loadArchive` (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:1008-1016) deliberately refuses a row whose `row.userId !== this.userId`, and its own doc comment gives the reason: "an id can be held across a sign-out and the listing is not the only way in. The answer for somebody else's archive is the same as for one that does not exist." The identical reasoning applies to `load(docKey)` (line 510), `changeCount(docKey)` (line 1162) and `storedSnapshotSize(docKey)` (line 1176), none of which consult the `userId` recorded on the `HeaderRecord` (line 69) — `load` returns the decompressed snapshot, meta and full change log for whatever sits at the key. The only protection is that the key is unguessable, and it is not: the store key is `{apiKey}/wb:{userId}:{docKey}/{docKey}` (durable-session.ts `durableClientKey`), where `apiKey` is `VITE_YORKIE_PUBLIC_KEY` shipped in the bundle, `userId` is the sequential integer `me.id`, and `docKey` is `sheet-<uuid>` etc. On a shared browser profile holding two accounts' entries, any caller that constructs a key rather than receiving it from the SDK reads the other account's document content verbatim. I could not find a currently-reachable caller that does so — the SDK only ever supplies its own key, derived from the latched `me.id` — so this is an asymmetric-guard / defence-in-depth gap rather than a live exploit, which is why confidence is low; impact if a future caller or a key-derivation bug reaches it is cross-account document disclosure. Fix shape: apply the same `header.userId !== this.userId -> undefined` check in `load` that `loadArchive` already applies.

samples.summary: `load()` refreshes `updatedAt`, so merely opening a document whose read authority was revoked renews both the 30-day retention backstop and the reconcile's `updatedSince` exemption
samples.evidence: `load` calls `this.touched.add(docKey)` and `void this.touch(docKey)` (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:532-537), and `touch` writes `header.updatedAt = this.now()` (line 565). Two cleanup paths key on that field: `collectStale` selects on `BY_UPDATED_AT` (line 1129), and `purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments` passes `updatedSince: listedAt` (offline-erase.ts:404) which `purgeDocument` uses to skip any entry with `updatedAt >= listedAt` (line 887-891). Consequence: a document in a workspace the user was removed from has its retention clock reset by the attach that merely reads it — the SDK loads before it writes — so the 30-day sweep, named throughout the design as the backstop for every other cleanup path, never fires for it; and because `OfflineRuntime` mounts alongside the editor route, an attach that lands after `listedAt` (stamped at offline-runtime.tsx:133) also wins the `updatedSince` exemption for that session. The effect is racy rather than systematic, hence minor, but it means the two mechanisms intended to bound how long revoked content survives can both be defeated by opening the document.

samples.summary: Store refusal errors embed the full SDK store key — Yorkie API key, numeric user id and document key — in exception messages handed to `onWriteFailure` and logged
samples.evidence: `refuseIfDisabled` builds `offline saving is switched off; "${docKey}" is not being stored` (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:384-387) and `refuseIfEvicted` builds `offline entry for "${docKey}" was evicted...` (line 715-718). `docKey` here is the SDK's scoped key `{apiKey}/wb:{userId}:{docKey}/{docKey}`, so each message carries the Yorkie API key, the signed-in user's numeric id and the document identifier. Both are passed to `this.reportWriteFailure` (line 388, and via `withQuotaRetry` line 1307/1313/1318) and rethrown; `offline-erase.ts` and `offline-runtime.tsx` `console.warn` store errors in several places (offline-erase.ts:258, 293, 327, 409; offline-runtime.tsx:97, 109, 141, 154). The repo runs Sentry (docs/design/observability.md, cited in the change as "no PII"), so any of these that reach an error reporter put account identifiers into third-party telemetry. Low sensitivity individually — the API key is the public one — but it is identifiers in error strings that did not need to be there; the doc key alone would carry the same diagnostic value.

samples.summary: Web Lock names encode `{userId}:{docKey}` and are enumerable origin-wide, exposing another account's user id and open-document keys to whichever session is running
samples.evidence: `durableLockName` produces `wb-durable:${userId}:${docKey}` (durable-session.ts, `durableLockName`), and `isOpenInAnyTab` reads every held lock via `navigator.locks.query()` and matches on prefix `"wb-durable:"` when no `userId` is supplied (durable-session.ts:~245-255, the `options.userId === undefined` branch). `navigator.locks.query()` is origin-scoped, not session-scoped, so on a shared browser profile with two accounts open in different tabs, account B's page script can enumerate account A's numeric user id and the document keys A currently has open. The change's own test asserts exactly this readability (`durable-session.test.ts`, "reports a document held by any tab as open" with `wb-durable:someone-else:note-7`). No document *content* leaks and the production callers all pass `userId`, so this is cross-account metadata within one browser profile rather than a content disclosure — but the identifier did not have to be in the lock name (a hash or an opaque per-session id would serve the election equally well).

samples.summary: `documentIdsIn` swallows every failure and returns `[]`, so a successful workspace delete or self-removal can silently purge nothing locally
samples.evidence: `documentIdsIn` wraps `fetchWorkspace` + `fetchDocuments` in `try { ... } catch { return []; }` (workspaces.ts:101-115), and both `deleteWorkspace` (line 128) and `removeMember` (line 160) compute `doomed` from it before the access-ending request. When the listing fails, `purgeOfflineDocuments(doomed, { dropArchives: true })` at lines 136 and 167 runs with an empty array and deletes nothing, while the server-side delete/removal succeeds. The full local copy — snapshot, change log and any archive — of every document in a workspace the user no longer has access to then stays on disk until the once-per-session reconcile happens to run and succeed, which is the same gap flagged in the recovery finding. The code documents this as "Best effort" and the design names the reconcile as the backstop, so this is a deliberate degradation rather than a bug; it is reported because the only two remaining backstops (the reconcile and the 30-day sweep) are each independently weakened by the other findings here.

samples.summary: Path-traversal regression assertion weakened from every-URL to some-URL for the encoded id
samples.evidence: The per-URL `expect(pathname).toContain(encodeURIComponent(TRAVERSAL))` was replaced by a single `paths.some(...)` check (url.test.ts:170-174), because `deleteWorkspace` now issues a companion `fetchDocuments()` request carrying no id. The load-bearing half — `expect(pathname).not.toContain("/auth/logout")` — is still asserted over every URL (lines 162-164), and since the fixture id is a `..` traversal, any un-`seg()`-encoded use anywhere would still normalise to `/auth/logout` and fail. So the traversal invariant itself is intact and the reasoning in the comment is correct. What is lost is the weaker "every request that carries the id encodes it" property: a second request that embedded the id raw but with a non-traversing payload would no longer be caught. Scoping the `.some()` to "every URL that contains the id's characters at all contains them encoded" would restore it without breaking on the companion request.

verdict.reason: The code is exactly as the finding describes. In offline-runtime.tsx the revocation reconcile (fetchDocuments + purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments with archives:"drop") sits in a try/catch at lines 114-142 that only console.warns, and offerRecoverableWork is invoked unconditionally at lines 146-155 with no record of whether the reconcile completed. Accepting the offer calls recoverOfflineCopy (offline-runtime.tsx:224), which creates a new server-side document from the archived content (offline-copy-recovery.ts:196, 210-211). purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments is the only mechanism that drops archives on the removed member's own device: removeMember gates its purge on isOfflineUser(String(userId)) (workspaces.ts:159), which is false on the remover's machine, and workspaces.ts:147-153 documents that the removed member's device relies solely on the OfflineRuntime reconcile. offline-erase.ts:356-358 states the rule this violates ("keeping one for a workspace the user was removed from would hand them a permanent copy of content they may no longer read"). The test suite pins the vulnerable behaviour: with fetchDocuments rejecting, purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments is never called (offline-runtime.test.tsx:167-175) yet the recovery toast with its "Save a copy" action still fires (offline-runtime.test.tsx:177-183, 215-225). I found no compensating guard on the recovery path — listRecoverableWork reads archives straight from the store (offline-copy.ts:58-68), describeArchivedDocument deliberately does not consult the server, and the fetchDocument title lookup swallows failures (offline-runtime.tsx:211-215). This is an access-control/revocation-enforcement gap in my lane (content outliving authority to read it, re-materialized as a user-owned shareable document), not a general correctness bug, so no refutation ground applies.

verdict.reason: The code is as quoted — `load()` (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:510-549) omits the `header.userId !== this.userId` check that `loadArchive` applies (:1008-1016) — but the cross-account read it is said to enable is unreachable. The store key that reaches `load` is always `apiKey/wb:{me.id}:{docKey}/{docKey}`: `durableClientKey` hard-codes the owner segment (durable-session.ts:80-81), the attacker-controllable `docKey` appears only after that fixed `wb:{me.id}:` prefix so it cannot be crafted to collide with another account's rows, and `collab-document-provider.tsx` puts `me?.id` in the election `subject` (:233) and only uses `decided` when `held.current.subject === subject` (:246-252), so a stale client key from a previous account can never be paired with a new `userId` — it falls through to the non-durable branch (:305-307). The store is constructed with that same `String(me.id)` (:311-312 → durable-yorkie-provider.tsx:135-176). Moreover `WafflebaseDocStore.load` has no application caller at all: the only non-test references in packages/frontend/src are the SDK contract helper (doc-store-contract.ts) and an unrelated `store.load(worksheet)` in history/revision-preview.tsx:470; `changeCount` is used only internally in a deletion path (:1376) and `storedSnapshotSize` only in tests. The asymmetry with `loadArchive` is principled — archive ids are auto-increment integers carrying no identity (:88) with a UI recovery path (offline-copy.ts:154) — whereas a live entry's key embeds its owner. Additionally, anyone with script/devtools access to the shared profile can read the same bytes straight from IndexedDB, so this class method is not the protecting boundary. The reviewer themselves found no reachable caller; this is defence-in-depth hardening, not a reachable authorization bypass.

finding.summary: Durable Yorkie client key is deterministic (`wb:{userId}:{docKey}`) while `ActivateClient`/`DeactivateClient` are authorized on token validity alone — any valid Yorkie token can hijack or tear down another user's per-document client row
finding.evidence:
`durableClientKey()` builds the Yorkie `ClientOptions.key` as `wb:${userId}:${docKey}` (durable-session.ts:80-82). Both inputs are readily obtainable: `userId` is the sequential numeric `me.id`, published to every workspace member via `WorkspaceMember.user.id` (packages/frontend/src/api/workspaces.ts:23), and `docKey` is `sheet-<documentId>` / `doc-<id>` etc., with `documentId` visible in URLs and listings. The key is passed straight through `CollabDocumentProvider` -> `DurableYorkieProvider` -> `KeyedYorkieProvider` as `clientKey` (collab-document-provider.tsx, durable-yorkie-provider.tsx).

Yorkie identifies a client row by `(projectID, clientKey)` upsert — that is precisely the property this feature relies on for a reload to resume the same actor. But the auth webhook binds nothing: `CLIENT_METHODS = new Set(['ActivateClient','DeactivateClient'])` and `if (CLIENT_METHODS.has(method)) return ALLOW;` (packages/backend/src/document/yorkie-auth.controller.ts:69, 246-248), documented as "No document. Validate token only" (docs/design/yorkie-auth-webhook.md:82). Nothing compares the token's `sub` against the requested client key.

Attack: obtain any valid Yorkie token — `GET /auth/yorkie-token` with any account, or the fully public `POST /auth/yorkie-token/share` with any share link (packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:87-95, no session required). The project public key (`VITE_YORKIE_PUBLIC_KEY`) and `VITE_YORKIE_RPC_ADDR` ship in the bundle. Then `new Client({apiKey, authTokenInjector, key: 'wb:<victimId>:<sheet-docId>'}).activate()` seizes the victim's client row, and `.deactivate()` tears it down server-side. The victim's durable client then shares/loses its actor and checkpoint state — the exact `clientSeq` collision and actor-keyed pull-dedup failure the design itself names as "silent edit loss" — and with the store attached this drives the SDK's `LocalChangesDropped` (`actor-mismatch` / `document-purged`) paths, discarding the victim's unsent offline wor

verdict.reason: Every element of the claim is present as described. `durableClientKey()` builds the Yorkie ClientOptions.key as the fully deterministic `wb:${userId}:${docKey}` (durable-session.ts:80-82), with userId being the plain account id (collab-document-provider.tsx:205) and docKey being `<type>-<documentId>`; it flows unchanged to KeyedYorkieProvider (use-durable-document.ts:249, collab-document-provider.tsx:305-311, durable-yorkie-provider.tsx:45-51). On the server side ActivateClient/DeactivateClient are allowed on token validity alone (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:69, 245-248) and the webhook payload has no client-key field at all (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:23-27), so nothing binds the requested client key to the token's subject — a grep of packages/backend/src for clientKey/client_key finds no such check anywhere. Valid Yorkie tokens are cheap to obtain, including via the unauthenticated POST /auth/yorkie-token/share (auth.controller.ts:87-95). That leaves a guessable, unbound server-side resource identifier (the per-(project,clientKey) Yorkie client row) that any token holder can activate or deactivate on behalf of another user — an IDOR-class authorization gap with data-integrity/loss impact, squarely in the security lane. The only mitigating factor I found is the build capability pin (yorkie-capabilities.ts:76-82 with @yorkie-js/react 0.7.22 < MinClientKeyVersion 0.7.23, injected at vite.config.ts:414-418) which currently keeps the durable path from mounting; that is a feature-version gate explicitly designed to be lifted by a dependency bump, not an access-control guard, and the required fix (an unguessable or server-bound client key) lives in this code, so it does not justify dropping the finding.

finding.summary: Recovery offer runs even when the access reconcile failed, so archived content from a workspace the user was removed from can be materialized into a new server-side document they own
finding.evidence:
`purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments` is the only mechanism that removes content from the *victim's* device after somebody else revokes access (offline-erase.ts:334-341 documents this). In `OfflineRuntime`, the reconcile is wrapped in `try { const accessible = await fetchDocuments(); ... } catch (err) { console.warn(...) }` (offline-runtime.tsx:114-142) and control then falls through to `offerRecoverableWork(...)` at line 150. The new test `'keeps sweeping when the reconcile fails'` (offline-runtime.test.tsx) explicitly asserts the recovery toast still appears after `fetchDocuments` rejects.

So on any session where the listing fails (offline, transient 5xx, the 401 arm throwing `AuthExpiredError`), an archive belonging to a workspace the user has been removed from is offered, and accepting it calls `recoverOfflineCopy` -> `createDocument({title, type})` + `applyImportedContent` (lib/offline-copy-recovery.ts), turning a local remnant into a permanent server-side document the removed user owns. The design's stated rule is that "content must not outlive the authority to read it", and `purgeDocument({archives:'drop'})` exists precisely so a revoked archive cannot be re-materialized. The offer should be gated on a reconcile that actually succeeded. Confidence is medium because the user already possesses the plaintext locally; the escalation is that it becomes a durable server-side copy.

verdict.reason: Verified in-repo. offline-runtime.tsx:114-142 swallows a failed reconcile (fetchDocuments -> purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments) with only a console.warn, sets no flag, and control falls through to offerRecoverableWork at line 150 (only `cancelled` is checked, which a rejection does not set). The offer's onClick (lines 223-227) calls recoverOfflineCopy, which at offline-copy-recovery.ts:196 and 210 calls createDocument({title,type}) plus applyImportedContent/writeNote, turning the local archive into a durable server-side document owned by the removed user. The repo states the exact rule this breaks: offline-erase.ts:333-341 documents purgeRevokedOfflineDocuments as the only cleanup reaching the victim's device after someone else revokes access, and offline-erase.ts:355-358 says keeping an archive for a workspace the user was removed from "would hand them a permanent copy of content they may no longer read." The behaviour is pinned by offline-runtime.test.tsx:177-183, which rejects fetchDocuments and asserts the recovery toast still appears, while offline-runtime.test.tsx:167-175 confirms the purge does not run at all on that session. No guard makes it unreachable: the only server touch in the offer path, fetchDocument at offline-runtime.tsx:212, has its failure swallowed by a bare catch that only keeps the 'Untitled' fallback and does not skip the offer, so it does not act as an access probe. Not refutable as not-present, already-guarded, or out-of-scope: revocation enforcement is access control, and the escalation from local remnant to durable server-owned copy is a genuine weakening even though the user already holds the plaintext locally (which is why major, not critical, is the right severity).
